fields.title: The University of Victoria, UVIC
fields.body_html:
Since 1983, when we moved to beautiful Victoria, BC, I have had a deep affection for the local university students. There are a few different Christian ministries on the campus, and I have been involved with most of them, speaking at student gatherings, participating in prayer groups and, for several years, hosting weekly gatherings at my home.

I was invited to speak at one of the weekly meetings of Intervarsity Christian Fellowship (IVCF). I was happy to accept the invitation and, having prepared my message, arrived at the University building where the meeting was to take place. A student greeted me and then, rather sheepishly, asked if I could limit my time to half an hour as there had been a mix-up and another student had arrived from a campus “up-island”, anticipating that he was to be the speaker that evening. I responded that I would be totally willing for him to take the whole time and would not be offended at all. I enjoyed sitting in on this eager group of students as they fellowshipped around the Lord and His Word.

As in so many of my stories already told, this dis-appointment would turn out to be a stepping stone into future wonderful times with IVCF. I guess they might have felt a little indebted to me because, shortly afterwards I received a telephone call late one evening just after I arrived home from a church meeting. “Pastor Evans, would you be able to come and speak at our Christmas Banquet on Friday evening (two days away)? Our scheduled speaker is sick in Toronto and our leader is away with him at some conference. He phoned me earlier today to ask me to call you, but when I did so earlier, your wife told me you were out. I have tried several other pastors, but they all said it is too short notice. Can you please come?” When I answered in the affirmative (“but sanctify Christ as Lord in your hearts, always being ready to make a defence to everyone who asks you to give an account for the hope that is in you, but with gentleness and respect;” – 1 Pet 3:15 NASB), he was elated, and I heard a great sigh of relief. That was a wonderful evening with over 100 students in attendance. So I began my love-bond with IVCF (Intervarsity Christian Fellowship) and its leader, Jack D. Whenever I was home from my itinerant work, I would be supporting Jack in his work.

An interesting “coincidence” has just happened. I have not seen Jack for many years but, just as I was typing the above, my telephone rang. It was Jack. He was in Victoria for the afternoon and wondered if we might have coffee together! What a good time we shared reminiscing over those times of long ago. Coincidence? I think not. I prefer to believe it was “Godincidence” where the Father was expressing His pleasure at what I had written.

Some time later, after Jack had moved on to another ministry and another province, I became involved with a different campus work – UCM (University Christian Ministries) led by Tony J. Again, a close bond was formed, and Anne and I would host a gathering of 10–12 students at our home every week for a number of years.

My love for the students also took another form. I started a prayer walk every week, usually on Mondays, around the 2km circular road that defines the campus. Sometimes I had students walk with me, but I was mostly alone. I did this for about twenty years, hardly ever seeing anyone else on a prayer walk. Indeed, I even wrote an email addressed to all the churches in Victoria encouraging their members to take an hour out each week to do as I was doing – but with little known response (how sad!) – until a growing discomfort in my legs due to arthritis brought it to an end. I was stopped with bowed head, 200 meters short of my bus terminus, when a voice behind me called my name. It was Terri, leader of IVCF. So I began a new relationship as we met weekly at my home to pray together, until she left to marry Mike, one of the regular attendees at our weekly gathering.

Shortly after my final walk, a young man came to our church. I greeted him and asked, “What brought you here?” to which he replied, “You did!” He explained, “I have recently started a prayer walk around the UVIC campus with some other graduate students and professors. We have heard of the man who walked there every week, so I have come to see you for myself.” How my heart sang that my burden had now been taken up by others. God has His workers everywhere.

After Anne’s passing, I felt it was time to sell my home of 40 years. As I write this chapter, I can hear the buzz of electric drills and saws as workmen are upgrading my house for the new owners, due to take possession in one month. They are James and his wife Josie, whom you shall meet in the next chapter, and who have become such dear friends. You can imagine my joy to know that it is their intent to lease their house to students with IVCF under Terri’s leadership! The Lord’s name will continue to be praised here, and many will come to know Him in the rooms where I have prayed so long! Thank you, Lord Jesus!

fields.title: Books Are Multiplied
fields.body_html:
It is my custom, especially during my Quiet Time on Friday mornings, to reminisce about the journey the Lord has led us along. As I sit on my La-Z-Boy chair, under my quilt (my ‘meeting place’) to meditate, I think back to the ‘stepping stones’ of Betty’s question, to Don Evans, to Swansea University, etc., and frequently comment “Lord, You did that!” At the end of my lengthy ‘journey of remembrance’ I add the comment and prayer. “Lord, I have tried to sow Your seed wherever You have led me. Sometimes I did it well, but often I did it poorly. However, Lord, it is Your seed, and You said that it would not return to You without accomplishing its purpose. Please Lord, bring forth fruit from what I have sowed, somewhere in the world today. Amen.” One wonderful morning, He invaded my quiet place and showed me a far-ranging rice paddy field. Suddenly, green shoots shot up all over the place. I was thrilled and humbled as I considered what I think He was showing me. My labour was not in vain.

I have mentioned in a previous chapter the great blessings I received by hosting and mentoring, for a short time, Greg Gordon, the creator of www.sermonindex.net (see the chapter “Sermonindex.net”) – surely a God-placed ‘stepping stone’. I knew that he had put some of my sermons on the web page but had seldom taken the time to see how they were being received. That was until a couple of years ago. I was looking for some other sermons (by Stephen Evans) and saw my name nearby. I clicked and was reminded that 39 of my sermons had found their way ‘on-line’. Naturally, I looked to see if anyone had downloaded them. I would have been blessed to see a few hundred, maybe a thousand, downloaded. I was utterly amazed when I saw the figures – several times anything I had hoped for – surely the ‘rice’ was sprouting! But more multiplying was yet to come.

Six years ago, I received a call from a young man whom I knew by sight but had not yet become acquainted with. James asked if we could walk together as he wanted someone to be accountable to and to pray with. Thus began a deep friendship which continues to this day. His whole family have become part of my life, and I treasure every interaction with them.

We spent many hours walking, talking and praying together, for the church in Victoria and for personal needs. We have so many interests in common, but in many ways, we are so different. He is an entrepreneur of note, especially in IT, and has started up a number of companies. He also supports Pastor Dan Muwanguzi and his work in Uganda. (https://christianmodelministries.com/). On one of his visits to Uganda, James set up an IT company led by Dan’s nephew Isaac (www.odyssey.com), and for one of their early ventures they edited my current web page (www.garethevansministries.org). What a blessing! That blessing was multiplied as, for several months, I would present much of my Bible teaching each week on Zoom to all the employees. An extra little blessing came when Isaac’s wife produced their fourth child and named him Gareth!!

All my books were edited anew and made available for purchase through Amazon. It was James’ 14-year-old daughter Jaimee who designed all their covers, including this book. In appreciation for all they had done, I gave permission to the team in Uganda to use my books and any finances received for them, for the extension of their ministry.

It was my intention in 2024 to join James in Uganda to teach at one of Pr Dan’s many Pastors’ Conferences. As the itinerary was being made clearer, it became evident to me that my age and fragile body were becoming too large an obstacle to ignore. It would be presumptuous of me to expect my body to stand the strain of several hours driving on some Ugandan roads. However, my absence was not going to be a hindrance to ministry among those pastors, as Odyssey took the initiative to print my books locally and distribute them free to all the pastors in attendance. I understand that they have now been translated into four languages – English, Spanish and two local languages in Africa. I am truly amazed and so blessed to know that my writings are now being spread abroad just as my sermons are. Surely, the rice is “popping up” in the paddy field.

Lord, You are so good to me! May both the writing and speaking continue to be to the praise of Your Glory. (Eph 1:6, 12, 14).

fields.title: Lion’s Pride
fields.body_html:
My prayer times with James became a burden on my heart for the pastors and churches of Victoria, one of “the least-churched cities in Canada”. I made a list of the churches and their current pastors and began to pray earnestly one day a week, taking time over each one.

Since I came to Victoria, I have felt much like Caleb and Joshua must have felt, sitting in their wilderness tents, reminiscing over what they had seen in Canaan. They had sought to enter Canaan, but the unbelief of the other spies sent to scope out the land resulted in the Children of Israel wandering the wilderness for forty years. God still loved them and provided sustenance for them, but He was not pleased with them, having led them out of Egypt with the goal to enter Canaan, their promised land.

Victoria became my ‘wilderness’ after the miracles of Hazelglen Fellowship, M/V Anastasis and my fulfilment in itinerant ministry. Oh, there were times when I delighted in sampling the “quails and manna” so graciously provided, but I had tasted the honey and grapes of Canaan, and nothing less could satisfy my hunger. The church I attended became an oasis for me, but oases are found in desert places, and my vision was set on the mountains of Canaan.

In November 2024, I heard of four other pastors who, like me, had served the church for many years in Victoria but now came together weekly to pray. Like me, none of them was willing to ‘retire’ but felt a burden to continue serving the church by dedicated, fervent prayer.

At that same time, there was a major discussion among political leaders concerning “street people”. As Victoria has the mildest climate in all of Canada, it is a magnet for the homeless, drug addicts, prostitutes, brain-damaged, and others carrying various wounds of trauma. Let me call them “my people”, as I have assumed a priesthood for them before the throne of God (1 Peter 2:9). They have come to make Victoria their home, with a natural reaction from the residents and businesses among whom they dwell. The current debate was concerning the use of street drugs for patients admitted to our hospitals after overdoses or violence on the street. Should they be allowed or not? The Provincial Government held one opinion; the Federal Government had the opposite.

At my first meeting with my old friends, Neil B made a statement which had a major impact on me. “When is the government going to realise that they have no solution to the street problem? Only Jesus is the answer.” I took that as my cue, and the following Monday I ventured into the darkness of Pandora Ave, a street frequented by large numbers of street people. I entered Our Place, once set up as a Christian ministry but now having forfeited that role to be acceptable to the Government to receive government funding. I was impressed by its cleanness and the quality of its coffee.

I crossed the street to view a group of young people, dressed alike in leather jackets, who were ministering to drug addicts by providing a warming centre – this was November after all. As I began my questioning, a scream rang out. A young lady had just overdosed. As they rushed to inject her with Narcan to counteract the fentanyl (successfully) I was brought face to face with their leader, a thickset man covered in tattoos, with rings in his ears and on every finger, a medallion hanging around his neck and a mohawk hairstyle – he was everything I am not!

I probably stuttered a little as I began to speak. “Hi Jimmy, my name is Gareth, and I’m a pastor in this city. My heart aches for these people and, along with a few others, I am burdened with prayer for them – but we don’t know how to pray. Can you give me some pointers as to how we can pray, for we believe that Jesus is the only answer to the street ‘problem’?” Jimmy threw his arms around me and exclaimed, “Jesus is the answer!” When I questioned him further, he told me how he and his wife Megan had met Jesus a couple of years earlier and were now back where once they gave out drugs in order to bring the message of Jesus to the needy. “We once brought dope, now we bring hope!”

We adjourned to a nearby McDonald’s where, over cups of hot chocolate, he and Megan told me their story. Jimmy had had a life of violence and crime, had served many years in penitentiary, alternating with life on the street. Two children had been born to them and immediately taken away by the social authorities and put in foster care. When he left the penitentiary for the last time, Jimmy resolved to live a sober life in order to claim his children back – something that appeared impossible at that time.

He approached Rev Al Tysick, the only continuous Christian presence on the streets, with a request. “Al, I want my kids back. Please help me get my life in order.” Al arranged for them both to go to Vancouver to a rehab centre for some time and, from there, to a second faith-based centre where they both met the risen Lord. They determined they would return to the streets of “home” to help others find this pathway out of addiction and hopelessness.

Their lives were so radically changed that even the authorities saw the difference, returning their children to them after several years apart. Apparently, this was the first time this miracle had ever happened on the streets.

I’d like to put a little insert here concerning Rev Al Tysick. It was he who had worked at Our Place, formerly under the name of The Upper Room – a Christian ministry. I never met him but always had a high regard for him for, though not known to be of my evangelical persuasion, he was at least doing what Jesus would have done in serving the people of the streets.

When I met Jimmy, Al had already retired and had recently written a book about his experiences, Muddy Waters. I purchased the book and sat down one evening on my comfortable chair to spend an enjoyable, relaxing evening. Soon my comfort left me and the evening became heavy. I found myself crying freely, not because of the emotional stories I was reading, but crying in shame. I had lived forty years in this city and had, with my evangelical Christian brothers, turned a blind eye to the hurting on our streets while this “Samaritan”, not known to be in my theological clique, was doing what Jesus would do – washing feet, feeding the hungry and tending their wounds. That night I was changed. This 85-year-old, like Caleb of old, asked for the mountain where the giants dwell. Joshua 14. I could never again be satisfied with life in the oases of the wilderness.

As I sat at my computer one evening, I opened a folder titled “Prayer”. One of the files therein was written during the COVID crisis of 2021 when prayer meetings were by Zoom. My pastor wrote up this file in response to the evening’s meeting. As we had waited on the Lord for direction (something taught me by Ron Smith in Hazelglen days), I had seen a “beautiful white lily rising up out of muddy waters” – Al’s book is titled Muddy Waters. Was the Lord showing me what the future held? Are Jimmy and Megan that beautiful white lily?

I became a “dad” to Jimmy and Megan and have the privilege of mentoring them. They also called me “Kryptonite” as Jimmy starts crying whenever we embrace! They had very little knowledge of the Word but evidently a great “anointing” from God. I taught them Biblical fundamentals and began to draw other Christian leaders around them. One day I asked Jimmy what other Christians he had met working the streets. I know there are others, but his reply was genuine: “Dad, you’re the first Christian I have ever met!”

I have had the privilege of baptising them in the presence of their glowing, happy children. I walked Megan down the aisle and spoke at their wedding. I go on prayer walks with them and have no fear when embracing their friends. I have baptised three others in a tub on the streets in November weather! Because they have such great credibility among their people, I am accepted wherever I go and have been given the honorary title of “godfather”! God is doing something special on our streets, and I am so privileged to be a small part of it.

I anticipate this to be my final ministry – but one never knows. If God can open doors like these for me at 85 years old, what more can He do when I’m 90? I say to Him often, “O Lord, You have been so good to me over many years. Why should I doubt that You will continue to be good to me? I’m ready to come home but, in the meantime, please continue working in me that I might always be ‘to the praise of Your Glory’.”

Addenda: Should my reader wish to know more about Jimmy and Megan and their ministry, Lions Pride, I invite you to search their web page at www.lionspriderecoverysociety.ca or seek them out on Facebook. My own web page is www.garethevansministries.org, and my books may be found at www.ochorus.com
fields.body_text: My prayer times with James became a burden on my heart for the pastors and churches of Victoria, one of “the least-churched cities in Canada”. I made a list of the churches and their current pastors and began to pray earnestly one day a week, taking time over each one. Since I came to Victoria, I have felt much like Caleb and Joshua must have felt, sitting in their wilderness tents, reminiscing over what they had seen in Canaan. They had sought to enter Canaan, but the unbelief of the other spies sent to scope out the land resulted in the Children of Israel wandering the wilderness for forty years. God still loved them and provided sustenance for them, but He was not pleased with them, having led them out of Egypt with the goal to enter Canaan, their promised land. Victoria became my ‘wilderness’ after the miracles of Hazelglen Fellowship, M/V Anastasis and my fulfilment in itinerant ministry. Oh, there were times when I delighted in sampling the “quails and manna” so graciously provided, but I had tasted the honey and grapes of Canaan, and nothing less could satisfy my hunger. The church I attended became an oasis for me, but oases are found in desert places, and my vision was set on the mountains of Canaan. In November 2024, I heard of four other pastors who, like me, had served the church for many years in Victoria but now came together weekly to pray. Like me, none of them was willing to ‘retire’ but felt a burden to continue serving the church by dedicated, fervent prayer. At that same time, there was a major discussion among political leaders concerning “street people”. As Victoria has the mildest climate in all of Canada, it is a magnet for the homeless, drug addicts, prostitutes, brain-damaged, and others carrying various wounds of trauma. Let me call them “my people”, as I have assumed a priesthood for them before the throne of God (1 Peter 2:9). They have come to make Victoria their home, with a natural reaction from the residents and businesses among whom they dwell. The current debate was concerning the use of street drugs for patients admitted to our hospitals after overdoses or violence on the street. Should they be allowed or not? The Provincial Government held one opinion; the Federal Government had the opposite. At my first meeting with my old friends, Neil B made a statement which had a major impact on me. “When is the government going to realise that they have no solution to the street problem? Only Jesus is the answer.” I took that as my cue, and the following Monday I ventured into the darkness of Pandora Ave, a street frequented by large numbers of street people. I entered Our Place, once set up as a Christian ministry but now having forfeited that role to be acceptable to the Government to receive government funding. I was impressed by its cleanness and the quality of its coffee. I crossed the street to view a group of young people, dressed alike in leather jackets, who were ministering to drug addicts by providing a warming centre – this was November after all. As I began my questioning, a scream rang out. A young lady had just overdosed. As they rushed to inject her with Narcan to counteract the fentanyl (successfully) I was brought face to face with their leader, a thickset man covered in tattoos, with rings in his ears and on every finger, a medallion hanging around his neck and a mohawk hairstyle – he was everything I am not! I probably stuttered a little as I began to speak. “Hi Jimmy, my name is Gareth, and I’m a pastor in this city. My heart aches for these people and, along with a few others, I am burdened with prayer for them – but we don’t know how to pray. Can you give me some pointers as to how we can pray, for we believe that Jesus is the only answer to the street ‘problem’?” Jimmy threw his arms around me and exclaimed, “Jesus is the answer!” When I questioned him further, he told me how he and his wife Megan had met Jesus a couple of years earlier and were now back where once they gave out drugs in order to bring the message of Jesus to the needy. “We once brought dope, now we bring hope!” We adjourned to a nearby McDonald’s where, over cups of hot chocolate, he and Megan told me their story. Jimmy had had a life of violence and crime, had served many years in penitentiary, alternating with life on the street. Two children had been born to them and immediately taken away by the social authorities and put in foster care. When he left the penitentiary for the last time, Jimmy resolved to live a sober life in order to claim his children back – something that appeared impossible at that time. He approached Rev Al Tysick, the only continuous Christian presence on the streets, with a request. “Al, I want my kids back. Please help me get my life in order.” Al arranged for them both to go to Vancouver to a rehab centre for some time and, from there, to a second faith-based centre where they both met the risen Lord. Their lives were so radically changed that even the authorities saw the difference, returning their children to them after several years apart. It was he who had worked at Our Place, formerly under the name of The Upper Room – a Christian ministry.
